assignment_description:
Introduction to Joshua
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

PREP: The teacher may wish to read the article linked here that explains the genre of Historical or Historical Narrative books of the Bible. The focus is always on who God is (known as the theology of God) while the history of his people is told.
∞ Article Link: Introduction to the Old Testament Historical Books

➜ INTRO
This year in the Old Testament, we will read five books: Joshua, Judges, Ruth, 1 and 2 Samuel. These books continue the story of Israel so that when we open our Bible to the book of Joshua, it is as though we are starting to read in the middle of a story where important events and people have already been introduced and discussed.
In order to understand what is going to happen next, let's do a short review of what has happened so far. The first five books of the Bible are a group of books called the Pentateuch. The Pentateuch is the books of Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, and Deuteronomy. The next set or category has twelve books in it and is called Historical or Historical Narrative. We will read the first five of these books this year. Historical narrative books show us who God is while the story of his people, the Israelites, is told. When you read a historical narrative book, you will see that it answers the question, "And then what happened?"
What do you recall about what has happened so far in the life of Israel? (Students may mention Abraham, Moses, being in Egypt, plagues in Egypt, crossing the Red Sea, etc.)
Leaders of Israel have included Abraham, who received a promise from God that He would bless him with land, people, and many blessings.
Next, the nation of Israel was led by Moses. Moses led the people as they escaped from Egypt, crossed the Red Sea, and wandered in the wilderness. 
God made a covenant (promise) with Moses that if the people followed God, they would be blessed. But if they disobeyed, they would be cursed (things would not go well for them). For today's reading, we are going to read a passage from the book of Deuteronomy where the covenant God made with Moses is written about. As we read Joshua, Judges, Ruth, and First and Second Samuel, these promises will be underlying the decisions the people and leaders of Israel make, so it is an important chapter to keep in our minds as we read. Will they continue to follow God, or will they forget about him and turn to their own selfish ways? We will find out as we read the Historical Narrative books and find out the answer to "And then what happened?"

➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS
Deuteronomy 28:1-10, 15-19, 25

• What did God promise (or covenant) with the people of Israel?

➜ NOTEBOOK
This year, you will keep a notebook. Suggestions will be given in lessons for drawing or writing what you have read about, but you can always add drawings or writings of your own choosing as well.
Today, open up your notebook and create a title page with the heading: Old Testament.
As time and ability allow, write the names of the books we will be covering this year: Joshua, Judges, Ruth, I Samuel, and 2 Samuel. You can also write the genre of these books: Historical Narrative

Joshua Commissioned
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook, Student Bible Atlas

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about the intro to Joshua from last time?

➜ INTRO
Before he died, Moses passed on the leadership of the people of Israel to Joshua (Deut. 31:7-8). In today's reading, Joshua will speak to the people about entering the Promised Land—the nation of Canaan. As Joshua speaks, he reminds the people of what they should do to have success and blessings. He also says, "Be strong and courageous." The reason the people could be strong and courageous is because the Lord was going with them and preparing their way. As we read, count how many times you hear this phrase or words similar to this.

➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS
Joshua 1:1-18

• How many times did he say "Be strong and courageous"? Why do you think he repeated that command?
• How would you feel if you were an Israelite about to enter the Promised Land?

➜ MAP WORK
⍞ Map Resource: Student Bible Atlas p.8-9 Maps 4 and 5
1\. At the end of Deuteronomy, we are told that before he died, Moses "went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo" (Deut. 34:1) and was shown the Promised Land. On Map 4 (the larger map), locate Moab, the Jordan River (labeled as "R. Jordan"), and Canaan.
2\. Look at the image in the bottom right-hand corner to see the view from Mount Nebo.
3\. Looking at Map 5, locate Mt Nebo and the Jordan River. Follow the arrows to see the direction the Israelites will move forward in the book of Joshua. The Jordan River moves north to south, and to the east is a plateau (mostly flat, level ground) and mountains to the left. The people are approaching Canaan from the south. The first move they will have to make is to cross the Jordan River.

➜ NOTEBOOK
In your notebook, create a title page for the book of Joshua.
Draw a picture of Joshua speaking to the Israelites as their new leader. As time and ability allow, write the phrase "Be strong and courageous." Older students might write a short summary of the passage or a key verse from the passage.

Rahab Hides the Spies
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible; Manners & Customs of Bible Times

NOTE: Two different options are given for the reading from Manners & Customs. Choose which one best fits the age or the interests of your student(s). This book will be used throughout the year to give background explanation of the customs of the people at the time. Because the book covers the entire Bible, at times other verses will be referenced, but selections have been chosen to give background to the Old Testament books we are reading.

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
Joshua is going to send two spies into the land to check it out. Maybe he thought back to how he had once been a spy for Moses!

➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS
Joshua 2:1-24

• Deuteronomy 28:10 says, "And all the peoples of the earth shall see that you are called by the name of the Lord, and they shall be afraid of you." How does what Rahab says and does agree with (or prove) this verse from Deuteronomy? (If needed, see Josh. 2:9-11, 24)
 
➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS
Rahab's family lived in a house that was part of the walls of Jericho. Read the following passage for an idea of what this may have looked like.
Manners & Customs "Brick Houses"
Younger students: View the illustrations and read p.28 "When the semi-nomadic" - "stone was white."; p.30-31 "The flat roof" - "in Matthew 24:17."
Older students, or as time and interest allow: View the illustrations and read p.28-31 "When the semi-nomadic" - "in Matthew 24:17."

Crossing the Jordan
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read in Joshua last time?

➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS
Joshua 3:7-17; 4:15-24

• How would the stones help the children (or future generations) remember what happened at the Jordan River? If you were there and someone asked you what the stones were for, what would you answer?
• What do God's miracles tell us about God?

➜ NOTEBOOK
Draw a picture or write a short summary of today's passage. Older students may pick a key verse or phrase from today's reading to write as well.

The Walls Fall
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS
1\. Israel celebrates Passover and remembers how God has delivered them from Egypt.
Read Joshua 5:10-15.

• In verse 12, it says the manna stopped. How do you think the Israelites felt about that?

2\. Read Joshua 6:1-19.
Jericho is the first city the Israelites need to conquer, as Jericho protects the entry into the land from the east, where they crossed the Jordan. Scholars say Jericho "was about a twelve-acre site...[and] Based on the size of the site today, it seems that it might have taken Joshua's army less than half an hour to march around the city walls...In the ancient world every war was holy war because people believed that their gods called them to war, led them in battle, and fought on their behalf...For this assault it was the ark and the priests that gave indication of God's presence with the Israelites and made it plain that the battle belonged to the Lord." (Bible Story Handbook, Walton) Usually, when an army defeated a city or people, they would take the plunder or goods (such as jewelry and anything that was worth a lot). In this case, the people did not take anything, because it wasn't they that claimed the victory—it was God who won this battle.

➜ VIEW
∞ Video Link: Sound of the Shofar
View the video showing various Jewish people blowing the shofar, the ram's horn trumpet that was used in Israel's history—and is still used today—to call people to worship. What would it have been like to hear this sound if you were part of the army marching around Jericho?

➜ NOTEBOOK
Draw a picture or write a short summary of what you read today. Older students might write out a key verse from this passage or write a longer summary.

Achan's Sin
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible; Manners & Customs

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
Last time, we saw that the people did not take any of the plunder from Jericho as they were directed by God: "But all silver and gold, and every vessel of bronze and iron, are holy to the Lord; they shall go into the treasury of the Lord." (6:19) The word "plunder" means the valuables or possessions that would be taken from the people defeated in war. Armies that won battles would take the plunder not only to celebrate the victory, but to add the loot to their money pile so they could afford to keep battling! After the battle at Jericho, everyone followed this rule and listened...except Achan.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Joshua 7:1-25
"When Achan took goods as plunder, it was like making a claim that the Israelites had won the battle rather than the Lord."

➜ READ & DISCUSS
Manners & Customs of the Bible "War and religion" (See note above.) p.268-269 "It was not" - "his own people."

Preview Manners & Customs reading regarding warfare. Either summarize or skip the couple of sentences that may not be appropriate for younger students.

assignment_description:
Tricked
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
Two events happen in today's passage. Do you recall what genre the book of Joshua is? (Historical Narrative) In a narrative (story), events are told as though someone is asking, "And then what happened?"
First, Joshua renews the covenant that God had given to Moses. Do you remember what God promised Moses? (Deut. 28 - If you follow and obey God, then you will be blessed. If you do not follow or obey God, then you will be cursed, and things will not go well.)
As we read the story, we might ask, "And then what happened?"
Next, some kings in the land of Canaan come up with a sneaky plan to trick the Israelites. In this context, a "king is the ruler of a single city," and these cities were starting to worry about the Israelites. Why do you think they were worried?

➜ READ & NARRATE
Joshua 8:30-9:15

• Why do you think it is good for Joshua to renew the covenant God had made with Moses and remind the people what God had said?
• The Gibeonites dressed in old clothes and brought stale food to try to give the impression that they had traveled from a faraway land. Unfortunately, Joshua and the Israelites "did not ask counsel from the Lord" (9:14). Now they are in a treaty with people from the land of Canaan. What do you think will happen?

The Sun Stands Still
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
The Gibeonites have tricked Joshua, but he will remain faithful to the treaty he made with them. Five kings in the land of Canaan decide to come fight against the Gibeonites because now they are all getting worried about the strength of Gibeon and of the Israelites. Next, the Historical Narrative book of Joshua will answer the question, "And then what happened?"

➜ READ & NARRATE
Joshua 9:16-21; 10:1-14

➜ VIEW & DISCUSS
∞ Image Link: Joshua Commanding the Sun to Stand Still Upon Gibeon

• What do you notice about this painting? Do you see the people, and do you see Joshua? What do you notice in the sky?

➜ NOTEBOOK
Draw or write a short summary in your notebook about today's reading. Older students may choose a key verse or write a longer summary.

Conquering the Land
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, Student Bible Atlas

NOTE: Today's reading will cover three chapters, but it will skip verses for time's sake.

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
Today's reading covers three chapters of information about Joshua and the Israelites defeating various kings in Canaan. These stories of Israel conquering the Promised Land point to God's might and power in fighting for his people, Israel. They are in covenant with him. Do you remember what the word "covenant" means? (a promise) Because God _is_ faithful, he will _be_ faithful.

➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS
Today's reading is in two parts:
1\. Joshua 10:42-43

• Who did the fighting for Israel, and what is happening as a result? (All the kings are being captured.)

2\. Eventually, Israel captures all the kings, and they will have some rest from fighting. While there were many kings who were defeated, we will read just one of the lists of their names.
Joshua 11:23; 12:7-24

➜ MAP
⍞ Map Resource: Student Bible Atlas p.10 Map 6
Look at the map and note the red dashed line. What does the map key state this red line shows? (Area permanently controlled by Israel.) Do you recognize any of the names of cities on the map that you have heard or read about?

Dividing the Land
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, Student Bible Atlas, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
Joshua chapter 13 all the way through chapter 21 lists how Joshua divided up the land between the tribes of Israel. After all, the book of Joshua "shows how God kept his covenant promise to give the land to Israel. He prepared them to enter Canaan, sent his commander to lead them, provided aid in battles, distributed the land, and renewed the covenant. The division of land, though not much of a story, is an incredible climax of the process that had brought the Israelites from their slavery in Egypt to the land that God had promised to Abraham through the covenant made over four centuries earlier. This is fulfillment of covenant promise on a grand scale." (Bible Story Handbook)

➜ READ & NARRATE
Our reading will be in three parts:
1\. Read Joshua 14:1-5.
2\. Read Joshua 16:1-10. Chapter 16 is an example of what these chapters list as far as boundaries of the inherited land that each tribe received. Other chapters define the boundary of the other tribes' lands.
3\. Read Joshua 21:43-45. These verses give a summary of the purpose of the entire book of Joshua. They could be called the Key Verses or Main Verses of the book.

• How would you summarize the purpose of the book of Joshua according to these verses?

➜ READ
⍞ Map Resource: Student Bible Atlas, p.11 Map 7 "Dividing the Land"
On the map, find the area that was given to the tribe of Ephraim that you read about in chapter 16. Locate the Jordan River. Why would it be good to have your land inheritance touch water?

➜NOTEBOOK
Draw a picture or write a short summary of today's reading. Older students may consider copying down the key verses of Joshua (21:43-45) or writing a summary of today's reading.

Joshua Gets Ready for Goodbye
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible; notebook; Manners & Customs of Bible Times

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
In the first verse of today's reading, Joshua states that he is now old. He gives the first of two speeches to the people of Israel. Imagine you are Joshua. What would you think would be important to tell the people in one of your last speeches you will ever be able to give them?

➜ READ & NARRATE
Joshua 23:1-15

➜ READ & NARRATE
Although the people were moving into a land where some cities had walls and homes built (as we read about Jericho), tents were also still used at this time. Read the passages on tents and dwellings, and view the images on p.25 about how a tent was erected.
Manners & Customs "Dwellings" p.20-21 "There are two" - "Ahab for this reason.";
"The Tent" p.24-26 "The tent of" - "door of the leader."

➜ NOTEBOOK
Draw a picture or write a sentence about today's reading. Older students may draw, write a summary, or copy down a key verse (or more!) from Joshua's speech.

Meeting at Shechem
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
The first part of today's reading might make you think, "Hm, I feel like I've heard this before." God is speaking through Joshua to remind the people of Israel about their history. The story is given using the personal pronoun "I," which is used 18 times in these verses. "I took...I gave...I sent...I plagued...I brought...I delivered, etc." Speaking in the first person (by repeatedly using the word "I") in the telling of the history, God reminds the people who won the battles thus far and who brought them to where they are today as a people. "God reviewed the marvelous deeds he had performed for Israel's benefit...From first to last Israel's conquests, deliverances, and prosperity were because of God's good mercies and were not of their own making." (The Bible Knowledge Commentary)

"Now therefore" begins verse 14. The word "therefore" is an adverb that means "as a result" or "for that reason." In other words, the people had been reminded of God's leading, and now, as a result of that, they had a decision to make. Read the passage and see what it is they have to choose.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Joshua 24:1-15

• Because God had brought them that far in their story (or history), what choice did they now need to make?
• What do you think their response will be? (We will find out what their actual response was in our next reading.)

➜ NOTEBOOK
Draw or write a summary of today's reading. Older students may write a longer summary or write down a key verse from the passage.
Alternative Option: As time allows, a short summary of the entire book of Joshua can be written or discussed out loud. Questions could include: What happened in Joshua? Were the people following God? What was Joshua like as a leader?

The Choice
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible; notebook; Manners & Customs

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
We are coming to the end of the book of Joshua. Overall, the people have obeyed and followed after God in the book of Joshua. And, according to Deuteronomy 28, what will be the result of following after God? (The people will receive blessings in the form of having land, fruitful crops, lots of kids or growth of their nation, and things will go well for them.) Did they receive blessings as Joshua led them into Canaan? In what way(s)? (conquered enemies, inherited actual land for their tribes, food to eat, no more manna, etc.)

➜ READ & NARRATE
Joshua 24:16-33

• When the people say that they will serve the Lord, Joshua doesn't seem to believe that they are sincere or genuine. He says, "You are not able to serve the Lord, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God." What was Joshua emphasizing by saying God was a holy and jealous God? (God is the only God, and their loyalty cannot be divided between other gods and idols. It is not God plus something else.)
• Eventually, he tells them exactly what they need to do. "He had heard the pledge on their lips; now he challenged them to prove their sincerity by their works...There could be no mixing of allegiance to God with idol-worship. A firm choice had to be made then, as in every generation." (Bible Knowledge Commentary) At the end of the passage, Joshua—as the final act of his leadership of Israel—renews the covenant between God and the people. God would bless them if they followed him, and they would be cursed if they did not follow him.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Manners & Customs p.82 and p.86 (Skip the pages of maps) "When the Jewish" - "began to advance."

➜ NOTEBOOK
Draw a picture or write a short summary of Joshua renewing the covenant at Shechem. Older students may write down a key verse or write a longer summary of the back-and-forth of Joshua and the people.

Judges Begins
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
While the Israelites followed God as they entered Canaan, there were little seeds of disobedience showing up throughout the book of Joshua. Now, in the book of Judges, unfortunately, those seeds grow into full disobedience. The book tells the history of Israel over centuries, but the book also encourages the Israelites to obey and be faithful to God.

The word "judges" might remind us of a courtroom; however, at this time in history, the judges were "tribal or national leaders. Often they were military commanders." They would settle arguments and give advice to the people of their territory. "Since Israel had no king or other central political figure, the judges played an important role in Israel's survival." (Basic Bible Commentary)

Sadly, as the book continues, the Israelite's turn further and further away from God, and things are very dark and rather disturbing. Throughout the book, certain judges will be introduced, and we will focus on their stories.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Judges 1:27-36; 2:1-10

• One bad choice Israel made is not driving out the Canaanites completely, and now things start to spiral downward. Why do you think this new generation did not know the Lord or the work that he had done for Israel? How would you imagine Joshua (if he were alive at that time) would feel about this?

➜ NOTEBOOK
Turn to a new page to create a title page for the book of Judges. Write the title of the book, and what genre it is: Historical Narrative. Draw a picture or write a short summary of the passage. Older students may write a longer summary or write down key verse(s) of the passage, including 2:10.

Cycles
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
The Israelites have started worshipping false idols and have turned away from following God. And now a cycle (or a series of events that keep repeating) will start that will happen throughout the book of Judges. "The cycles (disobedience, punishment, cry for help, deliverance) show how God demonstrated his power and mercy by delivering his people time after time after his justice had demanded that he bring punishment." (Bible Story Handbook) Sadly, it is also obvious that the leaders of the Israelites are just as bad as the people. In the cycle, the punishment they experienced was in the form of oppression, being conquered by an enemy, or even being enslaved.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Judges 2:11-23

Othniel
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

NOTE: There are two options for the reading today. For the second option of reading (3:7-26), preview the passage, as there is an instance of violence as King Eglon gets stabbed. However, the story is also a great example of the humanity included in the Bible.

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
Today's reading introduces the first judge, Othniel. Recall that there are cycles in the book of Judges that involve disobedience, punishment, cry for help, deliverance. Each time that cycle happens, their decline into disobedience, idolatry, and sin is even worse. As we read, listen for those steps in the cycle.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Younger Students: Judges 3:7-15
Option #2: Judges 3:7-26

➜ NOTEBOOK
∞ Image Link: Cycle of Judges
Draw and/or label the cycle that is in the book of Judges. You can come up with your own words or use the following for the steps of the cycle: disobedience, punishment, cry for help, deliverance. An example is given at the link. (Your chart/cycle does not need to look exactly like this!) Older students can put verse numbers from today's reading about Othniel next to each step (i.e., Disobedience 3:7).

Deborah and Barak
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible; Manners & Customs

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜INTRO
Today's reading will introduce us to the next judge in Israel's history. The judges "were often as bad as the people. Deborah was certainly an exception to this, as she was a faithful prophetess and brought deliverance in association with the commander Barak...Deborah was first and foremost a prophetess, one who brought God's word to the people. People came to her for decisions because she would inquire of God for them. It is likely that in this particular instance they came to ask God what they should do about the Canaanite armies. She responded by sending for Barak and giving him God's orders." (Bible Story Handbook)

➜ READ & NARRATE
Judges 4:1-15

➜ READ & NARRATE
Over the next couple of lessons, we will read a few passages from Manners & Customs to learn more about how the armies and groups fought at this time of the Old Testament.
Manners & Customs "The horse" p.213 "The horses of" - "back to Jezreel."; p.145 "Iron was originally" - "for the Temple."
Optional: As interest or time allows, the entire passage regarding workers with metal could be read. This gives a short history of the development of metal being used in the times of the Old Testament p.143-145 "workers of metal."

Deborah's Song
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
Sisera went into battle confidently, knowing the Israelites were outnumbered and would seemingly be easy to conquer. But God used both human means (the swords of the Israelites) and divine means to defeat the Canaanites. Today's passage is a victory hymn written by Deborah. In it, we see further information as to the divine means God used to crush Sisera by sending a sudden flood to the Kishon River.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Younger students: Judges 5:1-15, 20-21
Older students: Judges 5:1-31

• In verses 20 and 21, torrent refers to a flood of waters that overtook the army. If you were driving in chariots, how would a sudden flood of a river slow you down?

➜ NOTEBOOK
Draw a picture of Deborah, Barak, or the battle they fought against Sisera, or write a short summary. Older students may write a longer summary or copy key verses down.
Optional: Try writing a short victory song or poem celebrating the victory of Israel over Sisera.

Gideon
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible; Manners & Customs

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
The Israelites experienced peace for 40 years under Deborah's judgeship (5:31b), but then their cycle of disobedience began again, and they were conquered by the Midianites. Let's ask the question that the books of Historical Narrative answer: And then what happened?

➜ READ & NARRATE
Judges 6:1-4, 11-24

• Why do you think Gideon asked for a sign?

➜ READ, VIEW & DISCUSS
∞ Image Link: Terebinth tree
1\. View the image of the terebinth tree, a relative of the oak tree.
2\. The Midianites were a semi-nomadic tribe, which means they traveled from place to place at times. So they liked to attack when the crops had been recently harvested (v.3-5).
Manners & Customs "The Gezer Calendar" and "Grain crops" p.86-90 (Skip p.88-89) "By the time" - "for warmer days.";
"Threshing" p.94 "The separation of" - "to his enemies."

• Take a couple of minutes to look at the schoolboy's calendar in the text box labeled "The Gezer Calendar." If you live in an area where crops are grown, how does your area's calendar match this ancient calendar?

Gideon and Tests
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
In today's reading, there are a few tests that take place. First of all, Gideon uses "the dew and the fleece for an oracle. In an oracle, a yes-or-no question was posed to deity, and some mechanism was designated for deity to answer...Since God had already sent an angel to tell him that he was supposed to lead the armies into battle, Gideon wanted to check to see if those orders were still in place." Once the normal result happened, Gideon flipped it because he still doubted. "So with great apology (appropriate, since God had already given instruction), he then asked for the indicator to be switched; having the fleece dry and the threshing floor wet. This does indeed show a lack of faith on his part." (Bible Story Handbook) The second tests have to do with how the warriors drink from the water. Gideon once again was being asked to put his faith in God, going before the Israelites to fight their enemies.

➜ READ & NARRATE
Judges 6:25-40; 7:1-11
(In order to keep the story together, today's reading is a little longer than usual. If additional time is needed to finish today's reading, the next lesson time can be used.)

➜ NOTEBOOK
Draw a picture or write a short summary of today's reading. Older students may write a longer summary or choose one or two main verses from the passage to copy into their notebooks.

However, in these final chapters of Judges, that pattern changes a bit. These stories are not what happened _next;_ rather, they tell stories of what happened _during_ the time of the judges we have been reading about.

In the final chapters of the book of Judges, no further judges are introduced. "No note of Israel's sin, of outside oppression, of a cry for help, or of God's provision for a hero-judge to save the people. These chapters are simply additional bits of history that the editor apparently did not want to leave out." (Basic Bible Commentary) The stories may have been used to show the moral decay the people had experienced during the time of the judges.

➜ READ & NARRATE

Today we will begin the book of Ruth, which begins with a verse saying the story took place while the judges were ruling. Elimelech moves his family away from the city of Bethlehem to Moab because there is a famine. Moabites were an enemy of the people of Israel, but in that land, Ruth, a Moabite woman, marries into Naomi's family and shows faithfulness.

Ruth is a short, four-chapter-long book that shines in the midst of the darkness, because the story of Ruth holds hope. While the book of Judges shows us God can still work through people who are disobedient, foolish, and selfish, the book of Ruth shows us what he can do through people who are faithful to him.

➜ READ, NARRATE & DISCUSS

• Samuel has now died. Imagine the life he lived—leading, judging, being a prophet, and helping put both Saul and David into their roles as king of Israel. What did you notice about Samuel's life and how he lived?

The Davidic Covenant
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
We have reached Second Samuel. When the book was originally written, it was all one book; however, it was so long that it couldn't fit onto one scroll, so the book was divided into two parts. In Second Samuel, we will now see David become king over Israel. The verses we will read today show how, now that "David had been anointed and had shown his mettle, the text develops over many chapters how David gradually gained expressions of support." (Bible Story Handbook) Once David is on the throne, God makes a covenant with him.

➜ READ & NARRATE
2 Samuel 1:2-4, 11-12; 2:8-11; 5:1-4, 17-21; 6:12-19

Davidic Covenant
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

NOTE: Today's reading is a bit longer, so the focus will be on the Bible reading.

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
God now makes a covenant with David. In chapter 6:2, the ark of the covenant has been returned to Israel and returned to a "central positioning." God will now bless the nation of Israel through King David. David wants to build a temple for God, which is not an unusual thing for a king to do for the god of the people; however, God says he will "establish a house (dynasty) for David...By separating the temple building from the covenant, it is made clear that David did not gain God's favor for his dynasty by building the temple." (Bible Story Handbook)
The last part of the reading is a prayer of response from David to God.

➜ READ & NARRATE
2 Samuel 7:1-29

David's Kindness to Mephibosheth
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible, notebook

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
David finds out that there was a member of Saul's family who was still alive. This was Mephibosheth, the son of Jonathan. David shows kindness and loyalty to the promise he had made to Saul and Jonathan that he would treat anyone in their family line well. David is following through on what he had promised.
Mephibosheth was allowed to eat at the king's table, which "was a way of indicating that someone was under royal protection and care. Whether that person actually ate at the same table or not, provisions or rations were supplied from the king's house." (Bible Story Handbook)

➜ READ & NARRATE
2 Samuel 9:1-13

• Why would a new king not want anyone from the last (or previous) king's family to still be alive? (Because he was in the line of Saul, he could take over the throne.)
• God had chosen David to be king, and much of what happens in these chapters shows that he is not winning power by making political moves or using strategy to gain power; rather, he is gaining the support of the people and is being affirmed as God's choice for the throne over Israel.

➜ NOTEBOOK
Draw a picture of today's reading or write a short summary. Older students may write a longer summary or copy down a verse or more from the passage.

David and Bathsheba
⍞ Materials: ESV Large Print Bible

➜ RECAP
What do you recall about what we read last time?

➜ INTRO
David was anointed as God's chosen for the throne and has shown thus far that he has character and wishes to follow God's leading. However, in today's story, David fails to make the right choice. He abuses his power and is held accountable by God for this failure.

➜ READ & NARRATE
2 Samuel 11:1-21
David used his power to "achieve his own sinful ends." As his decisions in this passage affect his family, he will experience much sorrow, reaping the consequences of his sinful choices.
